scope: Taxonomic split, morphological variation, field-identification evidence; no county-level distribution analysis

findings.issue: Distinguish M. texana from M. biuncifera without treating the latter as a synonym
findings.decision: Preserve M. texana as distinct from M. biuncifera. Original Barneby & Isely 1986 split is explained by UT Plant Resources Center; historical M. aculeaticarpa var. biuncifera corresponds to biuncifera, not texana.

findings.issue: Competing numerical descriptions for leaf-pinna and leaflet count
findings.decision: Document rather than silently normalize: Barneby & Isely (1986) as excerpted by UT: pinnae 1–4 pairs and longest pinna at most 7 leaflet pairs; UT's discussion citing Barneby 1991 reports M. texana 1–5(–6) pairs of pinnae and 3–9(–10) leaflet pairs. Thus broad population descriptions and a narrow comparison key differ. Do not use seven leaflets as an absolute cutoff.

findings.issue: Field ID against M. borealis and M. aculeaticarpa var. biuncifera
findings.decision: Favor combination of prickle placement, flower corolla lobing, pod structure. In UT Hays field comparison M. texana often has a prickle aligned below petiole; M. borealis prickles more randomly along stem. M. borealis petals separate nearly to base, M. texana petals united; M. aculeaticarpa var. biuncifera has more strongly constricted pod margins and more infrastipular prickles. These are tendencies, not single-character guarantees.

Kew accepts Mimosa texana; Mimosa borealis var. texana is an explicitly listed homotypic synonym. Other older names listed by LBJ Wildflower Center should be retained as source-attributed alternatives rather than used to merge taxa.

pending: Any edit to the learner's absolute seven-pair threshold should be backed by comparison design and provenance in a separate integration pass.
No specimen-level reidentification attempted; all existing photographs and image credits preserved.
